opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that tension was something we thought about a lot. At World Labs, the long-term mission is spatial intelligence: building models that can perceive, generate, reason about, and interact with 3D worlds the way people do. That's a decades-long research agenda. But we also felt strongly that you can't just disappear into a lab for ten years and hope it works out. You need contact with real users, real workflows, and real feedback, because that's what tells you whether the capabilities you're building actually matter.

So with Marble, the way we approached it was to ask: what's the slice of spatial intelligence that's already good enough to be genuinely useful today? And the answer was world generation. You give it a text prompt, an image, a few images, or even a rough 3D layout, and it gives you back a persistent, explorable 3D world. That's not the end state of spatial intelligence, but it's a real capability, and it already solves problems for people in gaming, VFX, film previs, architecture, and VR, where making 3D content is painfully slow and expensive.

A big part of it was being disciplined about output formats. It would have been easy to build something that looks amazing in a demo but lives in its own closed viewer. Instead we leaned into exporting things like Gaussian splats and meshes, so people could actually drop the results into the tools they already use, like game engines or DCC pipelines. That interoperability is what turns a research artifact into a product.

We also invested a lot in control and editing. Early generative models are kind of a slot machine: you pull the lever and hope. Professionals don't work that way. So features like Chisel, where you block out coarse 3D structure and let the model fill in the visual detail, or being able to expand and edit regions of a world, came from asking how people actually want to work. That separation of structure and style is useful today, and it also reflects how we think about 3D representations longer term.

The nice thing is that the near-term product and the long-term research reinforce each other. Every improvement in the underlying world model, like better consistency, bigger scenes, and more accurate geometry, shows up directly as product value. And seeing what people build, and where things break, feeds back into research priorities. So rather than a trade-off, we try to treat it as a flywheel: ship the capabilities that are ready, learn from users, and let that pull the research toward the bigger vision of models that truly understand and interact with the 3D world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating, editing, and improving 3D worlds, but does not identify modeling counterfactual changes over time as a needed capability.

r002.rationale: It presents Marble’s current product and user feedback as reinforcing and guiding long-term world-model research, supporting the ambitious spatial-intelligence vision.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we thought about a lot, because it's actually a tension that's pretty easy to get wrong in either direction.

When we started World Labs, the thesis was very long-term. Spatial intelligence, the idea that AI should understand and generate and reason about the 3D world the way it now does with language, that's a decade-scale research program. And the danger with a mission like that is you end up building toward some abstract future and never shipping anything, and then you don't actually learn what people want from the technology.

So the way I think about Marble is that it's the first point on that curve where the research became real enough that someone could sit down and get something out of it today. You give it a text prompt, or an image, or a few images, and you get back a persistent, explorable 3D world. Not a video that pretends to be 3D, but an actual world you can walk around in and that stays consistent when you look back at the thing you saw thirty seconds ago. That property, persistence, is what the long-term vision is really about, so shipping something that has it isn't a detour from the research, it's a test of it.

The balancing act was mostly about being honest about what the model can and can't do right now. Early on, if you just hand people a generative model, they type one prompt and get one shot and sometimes it's magical and sometimes it's not. That's not useful, that's a demo. So a lot of the product work was about giving people control. Multi-image inputs so you can pin down the layout you actually want. Editing tools so you can go in and change part of a world without regenerating everything. Composing worlds together. Those features exist because real users, game developers, VFX people, architects, kept telling us that generation alone wasn't enough, they needed to direct it.

And the honest answer is that those product constraints fed back into the research in ways we didn't fully anticipate. Making a world editable forces you to think about what the right representation is. Making it exportable, so someone can drop it into Unity or Unreal or a web viewer, forces you to confront the gap between a pretty render and a usable asset. Those aren't just engineering problems, they're research problems, and we probably would have deprioritized them if we'd stayed purely in the lab.

So I'd say the balance isn't really a tradeoff where you give up some long-term ambition to ship something today. It's more that shipping is how you find out whether your long-term thesis is pointed in the right direction. If people are actually building with the worlds, that's evidence the representation is right. If they aren't, you want to know that now, not in five years.

r001.rationale: The response discusses persistent worlds that remain consistent when revisited, but does not identify modeling counterfactual changes over time as a needed capability.

r002.rationale: It describes Marble as the first point where the research became useful in practice and says shipping it tests and informs the long-term spatial-intelligence vision.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the long-term ambition and the near-term usefulness reinforce each other. Spatial intelligence is a big goal, but people need something concrete they can do with it today. With Marble, that means focusing on creating worlds that people can actually explore and use, and making that experience useful even while there’s a lot left to solve.

Then the product becomes a way to learn. Where do people want more control? What breaks when they try to use a world for something we didn’t anticipate? Those questions help turn a broad research ambition into specific problems to work on. Ideally, the work that makes Marble better for someone today is also moving us toward richer spatial intelligence over time.

r002.rationale: It presents Marble’s current product as a way to learn from users, with improvements that also advance the longer-term spatial intelligence ambition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to have the long-term ambition guide what you build, but let people’s immediate needs tell you whether it’s useful. Spatial intelligence is a big goal, so you need to find a piece of that goal that delivers value today.

With Marble, that means giving people a way to create and explore a world, rather than asking them to care about spatial intelligence as an abstract capability. Can they get something interesting out of it? Can they use it in a creative process? Where do they get stuck?

Those questions also push you toward the longer-term goal. If someone wants to move through a space or change something in it, that exposes what the system needs to understand. So the balance is really about finding applications where making the product more useful also forces you to make progress on the underlying intelligence.
